title.narrative: GEM Program Global Child Project: Coordination and Knowledge Management

description.narrative: Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency.

Socio-economic Benefits167. The socio-economic benefits of the GEM Global Child Project (GCP) are integral to its theory of change and are clearly articulated in both Section A (Project Rationale) and Section B (Child Project Description) of this document. These benefits are not incidental—they are core to the project’s ambition to drive a just and sustainable transition in the electronics sector, particularly across low- and middle-income countries facing compounded environmental and development challenges.168. The electronics value chain is currently characterized by persistent socio-economic imbalances: informal labor in e-waste processing with little protection or social security (the majority of which are female workers with less entitlements to welfare and social protection, as well as lower pay on average); the gender gaps in access to formal jobs, training, and decision-making; and limited access to affordable, durable technology for low-income consumers. The GCP responds directly to these realities by generating both direct and indirect benefits that support structural transformation, market formalization, social inclusion, and capacity building (both within the industries and among local communities).Direct Socio-Economic Contributions 169. The GCP delivers tangible value through its targeted technical assistance, training, knowledge generation, and communication activities. These interventions build national capacity in sustainable electronics governance while enabling inclusive access to opportunities along the value chain. Specifically:• Capacity-building and training programs empower government agencies, private sector actors, and civil society with the knowledge and tools needed to implement circular electronics strategies. These activities also help develop specialized skills in repair, refurbishment, material recovery, and sustainable design—laying the groundwork for green job creation. Moreover, by integrating the gender-responsive dimensions into the training programs, the GCP ensures the inclusiveness and fairness of the socio-economic benefits to be shared among different gender groups of the society. • Gender-responsive guidelines and policy tools support the development of fair, inclusive regulations. By promoting safer working conditions, equitable participation, and enhanced representation of women—especially in informal or hazardous roles—the project contributes to long-term social equity, empowerment, and occupational health and safety, helping to reduce the global gender gaps in these regards. • Technical guidance on reuse, repair, and right-to-repair frameworks offers immediate consumer and economic benefits by lowering barriers to maintenance and extending product lifespans, reducing the need for new purchases. The emphasis on supporting the training of women workers and female trainers also particularly contribute towards female leadership and knowledge building of women as professionals, consumers, and community members. • Gender-responsive knowledge management strategy and contents will be co-generated and circulated by the global child project (together with the inputs from the national child projects). They will include summary of best practices and lessons learnt about how to gender mainstream the management of global electronics, as well as stories that feature and promote female role models as agents for change towards sustainability and circular approaches. They have direct socio-economic benefits in terms of promoting and celebrating women’s roles in science and technology, business, as well as across the value chain of global electronics. These knowledge management contents will also directly contribute to the knowledge bases of similar future projects. • The GCP’s gender-inclusive communication strategy also ensures a fair and positive representation of women’s roles in global electronic management. This helps rectify gender stereotypes and encourages greater female presence in related fields. Even where national child projects may be at different stages of implementation, these global resources ensure that all countries benefit from shared knowledge, tools, and platforms.Indirect and Systemic Socio-Economic Benefits170. Beyond immediate technical assistance, the GCP plays a catalytic role in enabling the successful implementation of national child projects, amplifying their potential to deliver broader, lasting socio-economic impacts. These include:• Formalization of repair, refurbishment, and second-hand electronics markets, creating decent work opportunities, particularly for youth and women, and reducing the dominance of unsafe informal operations.• Reduced reliance on primary resource extraction, particularly conflict minerals and rare earth elements, through improved material recovery and reuse. This not only mitigates environmental damage but also addresses human rights and labor concerns in mining-intensive regions.• Enhanced consumer affordability and choice, through greater access to second-hand, repairable, and upgradable devices—helping reduce the digital divide.• Lower public health and environmental remediation costs, by reducing toxic exposure associated with informal recycling and unsafe e-waste disposal. This benefits governments, local communities, and health systems, particularly in vulnerable urban and peri-urban areas.• Reliable guidance, close alignment, and smooth coordination in gender mainstreaming practices throughout the program (especially from the program-level to the project-level). The GCP will offer training on gender mainstreaming, deliver internal communication and channel of gender mainstreaming knowledge base, toolkits, as well as expectations, which in turn contribute to the gender equality in different country contexts and in the global electronics value chain. 171. These benefits—both direct and indirect—will be tracked through a comprehensive set of objectively verifiable indicators outlined in the project’s results framework. The monitoring system is designed not only to assess technical outcomes but also to capture social inclusion, gender impact, and long-term economic value, ensuring a full picture of the program’s contribution to sustainable development.
To facilitate coordination among GEM country child projects and other relevant stakeholders, and strengthen knowledge management and exchange in the electronics sector
